vignette:
Minh had been working late in the accounting office when he was taken from a street corner on his way home, a time he still remembered as ordinary right up until the moment it was not. He had been stopped by men he did not know, pushed into a vehicle, and held for days in a place where every sound seemed designed to erase his sense of time and safety. Even now, when he tried to tell the story, the sequence broke apart in his mind. The hardest part was that the memory did not feel like something that had happened to him; it felt strangely detached, as if it belonged to another man, a scene he could only watch from a distance. He would catch himself seeing flashes of the room, the hands, the concrete floor, but the order never settled. It came back like a film that played over and over, beginning and stopping in the same frightened fragments.

In the months after he was released, Minh found that certain moments pulled him straight back into the old fear. If someone asked him about the future—at work, about next year’s deadlines, or even something simple like where he might live after the divorce—he felt a surge of unease that was hard to explain to others. Talking to strangers was worse. A casual question from a new client, a phone call from an unfamiliar number, or standing beside an unknown man in the elevator could make his body tense before he had time to think. In those moments, he became convinced that danger could come from anywhere, and that you could never really know who would harm you. That belief hardened quickly into the way he saw people now, as though any unfamiliar face might conceal the same intention as the men who had taken him.

Those same moments also fed a deeper and more punishing conclusion. When the future came up, or when he was forced into brief contact with strangers, Minh found himself thinking that something inside him had been permanently changed for the worse. He did not speak about it dramatically; instead, he said it flatly, as if describing a fact he disliked but could not disprove. He compared himself to who he had been before the torture—more open, less watchful, someone who had once made plans without hesitation—and could only conclude that that version of him was gone. At times he also found himself angrily wondering why nobody had stopped it from happening, why someone else would not have found a way to intervene. That thought did not bring relief. It seemed to deepen his sense that he had been left undefended, and that what happened said something bleak about how little protection a person could count on.

The more these thoughts took hold, the more the memory itself seemed to seize him. When he was alone at night after finishing accounts for the day, the fragments came more easily, and once they started they would loop without resolving into a complete story. He could not place the events in order, and the lack of sequence made the whole thing feel even less like his own past and more like an invasion that had no beginning or end. Sometimes he would stop mid-task at his desk because a scene flashed so vividly that he lost track of the spreadsheet in front of him. He began checking his surroundings in a quiet, almost embarrassed way, scanning the office lobby, the parking lot, and the sidewalk outside his apartment for unfamiliar men. Yet the harder he tried to protect himself from the feeling that anyone might harm him, the more the old film returned, as if his mind had no room for anything else once the fear was activated.

Over time, Minh’s life narrowed. He avoided conversations with new people at work, kept exchanges with clients brief, and let friends do most of the talking when social situations could not be avoided. He had been divorced during this period, and though the separation had several causes, he knew his mistrust and distance had made it harder for his marriage to survive. Now he came for help because the pattern was no longer something he could keep to himself: the intrusive memories were disrupting his work, his dread of strangers was making ordinary errands exhausting, and any discussion of his future—his career, his loneliness, even the possibility of another relationship—brought the same tight conviction that he had been damaged in a way that would not reverse. What he feared most was that he would go on living this way, always braced for harm, with the past replaying and the future feeling impossible to trust.
